To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the expression of PD‐L1 on T cells in HIV‐infected individuals is increased compared to controls and that PD‐1 and/or PD‐L1 blockades can restore HIV‐1‐induced T cell proliferation.
the expression of PD‐L1 and PD‐1 molecules is increased in HIV‐infected subjects and the blockade of these molecules can restore the immune function of HIV-infected subjects.

HIV‐1 infection is associated with increased PD‐1 expression on naive, central memory and effector memory CD4+ and naive CD8+ T‐cell subsets and increased PD‐L1 on effector memory CD8+ T-cell subsets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of impaired T cell responses during HIV‐1 infections.
the study of the mechanisms of HIV‐1‐induced T cell anergy.
the role of PD‐1/PD‐L1 in HIV infection and their potential for therapeutic intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PD‐L1 may have a greater impact on HIV‐1‐inflicted immune dysfunction than PD‐1, and therefore may be a more promising target for therapeutic intervention.

HIV‐1 infection induces a significant increase in the expression of PD‐L1 in the CD4 and CD 8 T cell subsets, and this increase in PD‐L1 could play a major role in the impairment of HIV‐1‐ specific responses in the HIV‐1+ individuals.
PD‐L1 and PD‐1 are not the only negative regulators of T cells in HIV infection, and their blockade does not rescue anergy and impaired HIV‐specific responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PD‐1 and its ligand, PD‐L1 play a role in HIV‐1 pathogenesis.
PD‐L1 and PD‐1 blockade may be a useful strategy in the treatment of HIV‐1 infection.
the expression of PD‐L1 and PD‐1 is altered during the course of HIV‐1 infection, which contributes to the development of anergy and impairment of T cell responses to HIV‐1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PD‐L1 has a greater role than PD‐1 in HIV‐1‐associated T cell exhaustion.
PD‐1/PD‐L1 blockade does not improve HIV‐specific T cell responses, which are impaired by the virus.
the blockade of PD‐L1 but not of PD‐1 restores anti‐HIV responses.
